  • N: atramhasīs | ana milkīya | qūl-[ma] || taballuṭ | [d]āriš

  • Note: On the interpretation of u₂-bu-ut, see the commentary on OB III 21.

4b-5

  • N: m[a]kkūram | zē[r-ma] || napištam | šullim
  • T: “Spurn property, save life!
BabaMB1 o 4b-5. m[a-a]k-ku-ra-am ze-e[r-ma] | na#-pi₂-iš-tam# šu-ul#-lim

6-7

  • N: elep (|) teppušu | e[ṣ]eršī-ma || eṣerti | k[i]ppātim
  • T: “The boat which you will build, draw it out as a circular plan.
  • Note: The interpretation of e[ṣ]eršī-ma as an imperative follows [RN3182: 299]: “Draw out the boat that you will make/ On a circular plan”. We take eṣerti k[i]ppātim as a predicative complement (on this category, see the comment on OB I 1). [wasserman2020flood: 69] understands e[ṣ]eršī-ma as a first person, but also takes e-[ṣ]e-er-ti ki-[i]p-pa-tim as a predicative.
BabaMB1 o 6-7. MA₂ te-ep-pu-šu e-[ṣ]e-er-ši-ma | e-[ṣ]e-er-ti ki-[i]p-pa-tim

8

  • N: lū mithār | šidda[š]a | u pū[ssa]
  • T: “Her length should be equal to its breadth,
BabaMB1 o 8. lu mi-it-ha-ar ši-id-da-[š]a u₃ pu-u[s-sa]

9

  • N: lū ištēn (|) ikûm | kaqqarša || lū ištēn (|) nindanum | ig[ārātūša]
  • T: “Her base should be one ikû (ca. 60 m²); [her] hull (lit. walls) should be one nindanu (ca. 7 m) (high).
BabaMB1 o 9. lu-u₂ 1 IKU ka-aq-qa₂-ar-š[a lu]-u₂# 1 NINDA# i-g[a-ra-tu-ša]

10

  • N: kannū | ašlā || <lū> ṭamû | [ina lib]bīša
  • T: <Let> the cords – each one ašlu long – be woven [inside] it.
  • Note: Compare the reading of this line suggested by Finkel in his edition of the fragment ([RN1780: 359]): ka-an-nu aš-la-a ta-mu-u[r] ša [MA₂], “You saw kannu ropes and ašlu ropes/rushes for [a coracle before!].” The reading is problematic, as it would result in kannu used for the accusative, as noted by [RN2399: 253 fn. 6] or as casus pendens, in the interpretation of [streck2017review: 140] (“Ropes, each (one) ašlu long – (when) you have found (them) for [the ship(?)], then may somebody twist …”). [george2016review: 445] suggests reading ka-an-nu aš-la-a <lu> ṭa₂-mu-u₂# [a-na ŠA₃]-ša₂, “[Let] tapes, each 120 cubits long, be laced [inside] it.” [wasserman2020flood: 71] follows this reading, though he notes that ṭam/wû is unusual when referring to the preparation of ropes, as this verb virtually always refers to wool, textiles and braids (but note ušandû ana gišparrīšu iṭammi ebla, “The bird hunter plaits strands for his snare,” in Palm and Vine 21′; @url{/corpus/L/2/12}{L II.12}). All three interpreters note that ašlu is a measure of length making 10 nindanum, ca. 60 m. [streck2017review: 140] explains that the distributive suffix -ā (ašlā) indicates that each and every one of the kannu-cords must reach this length.
BabaMB1 o 10. ka-an-nu aš-la-a <lu> ṭa₂-mu-u₂# [i-na ŠA₃]-ša

11

  • N: liptilkum | bītī | pi[t]ilt[am]
  • T: “Let my temple (personnel) twist the fibers into a rope for you
  • Note: For the interpretation of this line, see [george2016review: 445], who suggests reading the middle word as E₂{+bi-ti}, i.e., bītī: “Let my household plait the palm fibre into ropes for you.” George interprets this as Ea offering his temple personnel to help Atram-ḫasīs construct the boat. See also [wasserman2020flood: 72]. Compare the different interpretation offered in [RN1780: 359]: li-ip-ti-ik-kum GIŠ ar₂#-ti pi₂-[t]i-il-tam, “Let someone (else) twist the fronds and palm-fibre for you!”
BabaMB1 o 11. li-ip-ti-il-kum E₂{+bi-ti} pi₂-[t]i-il-t[am]
